q1.answer: ADR013 (node-fetch) is superseded and no longer in force; it was replaced by ADR014. ADR014 says all Node.js-executed code should use native fetch, while frontend plugins and packages (like NotificationsClient) should prefer the injected `fetchApiRef`, which is exactly why the constructor takes a `fetchApi` and no HTTP library is imported.

q2.answer: ADR007 (Use MSW to mock http requests) requires this for all fetch/XMLHTTPRequest calls in tests repo-wide. It says mocking via msw's express-style route handlers avoids each test having its own ad-hoc implementation of network mocking, and follows the pattern react-testing-library itself suggests instead of mocking fetch directly.

q3.answer: ADR006 cites that React.FC implicitly adds a `children` prop and does not support generic types on children. It notes the concrete fact that Facebook removed React.FC from the create-react-app TypeScript base template because it was an unnecessary feature with next to no benefit and a few downsides.

q4.answer: ADR010 names Moment.js as the alternative being replaced, citing two reasons: Moment.js is affected by large bundle sizes and has mutable-state issues, and separately Moment.js is being sunset by its own maintainers, who recommend switching to a modern alternative.

q5.answer: ADR004 (Module export structure) requires every exported symbol to be traceable through index files down to src/index.ts. It was meant to make it easy to answer questions like 'is this export also exported by the package?' and 'what is exported from this directory?'.

q6.answer: No — under ADR004's rule, a symbol is only publicly exported if it can be traced through index files all the way to src/index.ts; since notificationLinks.ts and plainText.ts have no src/utils/index.ts and are never mentioned in src/index.ts, that traceability chain is broken, so by the rule they are not part of the public API even though nothing explicitly marks them private — the absence of a re-export chain itself is what makes them private.

q7.answer: ADR011 defines `x-react` as the package for shared widgets, hooks, and similar code that both the plugin itself and third-party frontend plugins can depend on. A `-react` package only becomes justified once other frontend plugins need to depend on notifications' components/hooks; this plugin's code would need to be used by third-party plugins (not just internally) before splitting it out.

q8.answer: The one exception ADR003 allows is `React.lazy` modules, which require a default export. The workaround for teams wanting to avoid even that is to use `React.lazy(() => import('../path/to/Component').then(m => ({ default: m.Component })))`, converting a named export into the shape React.lazy expects without the module itself declaring a default export.

q9.answer: ADR015 defines the `loader`/`component` option pattern for providing JSX elements and components. Its Consequences section states they will update all APIs for the new frontend system (`@backstage/frontend-*` packages) but will NOT update any existing APIs for the old frontend system (`@backstage/core-*` packages) — meaning pre-existing code like the dev app's direct wiring will not be retrofitted.
